newsitem.title: UK: Capital markets rule in Eastern Europe.
newsitem.headline: Capital markets rule in Eastern Europe.

text.p: The deluge that has devastated parts of Poland and the Czech Republic seems to show there is a grain of truth in Shakespeare's assertion that "when troubles come, they come not single spies but in battalions."
Whether one believes in fateful coincidence or not, the fact is that the floods followed and prolonged a currency turmoil in both countries.

Analysts believe that apart from biting into gross domestic product growth and creating an inflationary impulse, the damage to crops and assets is likely to make it more difficult for politicians in Prague and Warsaw to carry out policy adjustments that the currency problems require.

Professor Stanislaw Gomulka, emerging markets specialist at the London School of Economics, says that although the slowdown in growth will hurt, especially the Czech Republic, problems the floods pose for policy are much more important.
"The reconstruction (of the stricken areas) will worsen the situation because it will create additional demand and bigger imports," he said.

Monetary relaxation through increased government borrowing and grain imports in both countries will have an adverse effect on what formed the backbone of the Czech economic crisis -- growing fiscal and trade deficits boosted by surging demand.
HOW THE CRISIS STARTED

As growth slowed in the first quarter and budget and current account deficits swelled, investors, who had ignored warning signals for too long and put billions of dollars of hot money into Czech assets, started a rapid pull-out.

The withdrawal sucked in without trace about $3 billion that the authorities were prepared to spend to defend their currency, the crown. Analysts say it is impossible to defend successfully a currency perceived as grossly overvalued and undermined by a faltering economy.
Realising that the battle would be lost inevitably, the authorities allowed the crown to fall and rushed to implement long-overdue structural reforms and fiscal austerity.
Poland's case is slightly different. Despite a ballooning trade gap, its fast-growing economy is in better shape and it had gone further in structural reforms than its southern neighbour.
Yet the zloty came under pressure too as investors began to believe that unless serious steps were taken soon, a Czech-style crisis would be likely within two years.
"What happened to the zloty can be seen as a warning signal and the market really did not want to test its (14 percent fluctuating) band," said David Lubin, emerging markets analyst at HSBC bank.
"The lesson ought to be that you take seriously such warning signals and tighten policies."
MARKETS RULE

The depth of the currency turmoil took the authorities in Prague and Warsaw by surprise and showed just how much international markets were capable of directing economic policy everywhere in the region.

Unlike policymakers in Latin America and Asia, where investors have in the past frequently administered heavy punishments for bad policies, politicians in Eastern Europe have, until now, failed to appreciate the extend of investment in their currencies and stocks.

"These economies are very integrated with international capital markets," said Lubin. "It's a loss of autonomy among emerging markets' policymakers which puts their economies at the mercy of capital markets."

A simple answer to that might be to restrict foreign access to stocks and currencies, if only temporarily. Yet most countries in the region aspire to either join or trade with the European Union and that will be impossible without opening their markets.
The advantages of opening up are higher confidence, bigger trade, more developed markets and access to cheaper money, which in the long run provides rather than limits stability.
The issue of when to open up is therefore crucial. Hungary, whose economy hit the rocks in 1995, has restricted access to its markets and concentrated on restoring macroeconomic stability.
Its stabilisation programme was hugely successful and although the economy still grows more slowly than that of Poland, the outlook is much brighter.
Miranda Xafa, senior analyst at Salomon Brothers, says Hungary has reached a level of stability at which it should start opening up its market.
"They could keep some restrictions but get rid of others," she said.
PATTERNS IN EMERGING MARKETS CRISES

Analysts agree that Poland may yet avoid trouble, mainly because it is most advanced in reforms. Uniquely in the region, its economy returned to output levels of before the depression that followed the collapse of communism in the early 1990s.
The private sector is booming, huge chunks of former state firms have been sold increasing efficiency, and a large part of the credit boom and worrying imports go towards revamping its industries.

"(Poland's) labour productivity...rose by an annual 13 percent (in the last three years), suggesting that the country's performance in structural reform was one of the best in the world," Credit Suisse First Boston investment bank said in a July research note.
Another difference is that Polish firms have borrowed less, especially abroad, compared to Czech firms.

Salomon's Xafa believes rapid credit growth can be one of the chief causes of currency problems if they fail to produce efficiency gains and higher exports, which happened both in Thailand and the Czech Republic.

"One of the reasons why pressures develop on currencies is excessive growth of credit," she said. "But the lesson is not that companies should not borrow abroad. The key issue is what they borrow for."
LSE's Gomulka believes that Poland may escape unhurt next year if it manages to discourage firms from tapping foreign markets excessively and at the same time erases its budget gap.
So far the government seems as reluctant as it has been during its four years in power in which period the deficit has stayed high and consumer demand allowed to soar.
Poland's ruling left, facing an election in September, assumed growth and economic success could be taken for granted.
"I call it a sin of complacency," says Gomulka.
He believes that successful transition economies sooner or later run into current account problems and must undertake bold corrective measures.

This is because growth, apart from creating confidence that makes governments less eager to carry on with reforms, boosts imports of consumer and investment goods. If at the same time hot money flows in, financing the gap, it is a recipe for disaster.

A policy response must inevitably be fiscal and monetary tightening to slow consumer demand and eliminate budget deficits, but these politically risky moves are usually put off by decision makers until its too late.

Ironically, the ensuing crisis almost always forces the authorities to introduce austerity measures of greater severity than were needed only a few months earlier. That was Hungary's case in 1995 and the Czech Republic's this year.
Poland can still escape if it acts after the elections at the latest. Others, including Russia -- the darling of hot money this year, should be already preparing responses, analysts say.
LESSONS LEARNT SO FAR
Russia's macroeconomic progress has been impressive, with inflation falling rapidly and some improvement in its fiscal balance. The outlook for the rouble is fairly stable in the short term.
Those factors, coupled with a much brighter political outlook, have led to two developments that, although broadly positive, can create problems.

First, stock and debt prices are soaring on foreign inflows, and second, flight of domestic capital -- estimated by some at up to $60 billion in the last few years -- has virtually stopped. If that capital begins to return, the pressure on the rouble to appreciate will increase, in turn attracting more and more of hot money into the country.
If the rouble appreciates much, expectations of a devaluation may rise. Add any political trouble to the formula, and capital withdrawal on a scale unseen in other emerging markets looks possible.
"On the basis of this logic (that there is a pattern in emerging markets) the Russian currency crisis is still maybe three to four years away," said HSBC's Lubin.

The fact that the rouble was hit by currency turmoil in 1994 has acted as a vaccine so far and if policy responses are accurate and the Russian economy finally begins to grow next year, the danger may disappear, analysts say.

They point out that recent speculative attacks on emerging currencies has not touched those -- such the rouble, Mexican peso, South African rand, Hungarian forint and South Korean won -- which had undergone a devaluation and a serious policy adjustment.
"It is as if markets believed that if you had your crisis already, you're safe," one analyst said.
